intro: Occasional longer explanations of topics in microwave photonics and analog circuit design, written for engineers who are new to them. Short tips sit alongside the longer notes.

notes.body:
A radio-over-fiber (RoF) link carries an RF signal as the intensity of light. You put a microwave signal on an optical carrier at one end, send it through fiber, and recover it with a photodiode at the other end. On paper the fiber is almost lossless and has huge bandwidth. In practice, the link's gain, noise figure, and dynamic range are set mostly by two components: the modulator and the circuit that drives it.

This note walks through why, using the most common setup: a Mach–Zehnder modulator (MZM) with direct detection.

The modulator's transfer curve

An MZM splits light into two arms, shifts the phase of one relative to the other with an applied voltage, and recombines them. The output intensity follows a raised cosine:

Pout = (Pin / 2) · [1 + cos(π·V/Vπ + φ)](1)

Here Vπ is the voltage that swings the output from fully on to fully off, and φ is the bias phase. For an analog link you bias at quadrature (φ = π/2), where the curve is steepest and the second-order distortion cancels. Around that point, a small RF voltage maps to a nearly linear change in light intensity.

Tip

Use the second harmonic as a bias monitor. At exact quadrature the second harmonic cancels. If it starts growing, the bias has drifted, so it makes a sensitive error signal for a bias-control loop.

Why Vπ dominates the link gain

The slope of the transfer curve at quadrature is proportional to π/Vπ. For an intensity-modulated link with direct detection, the small-signal RF gain scales as

G ∝ (π · Idc · R / Vπ)²(2)

where Idc is the average photocurrent and R is the source and load resistance. The square is what matters: halving Vπ buys 6 dB of link gain, the same as doubling the received optical power. Many passive analog links show net loss, often 20 dB or more, so this improvement has a direct effect on noise figure.

This is also where the driver comes in. In silicon depletion-mode modulators, Vπ·L is typically a few V·cm. A short device has a large Vπ, and a long one has more RF loss and harder velocity matching. The driver has to supply enough swing to use the modulator well without overloading it.

Pitfall

DC Vπ is not RF Vπ. Electrode loss and velocity mismatch make the effective Vπ rise with frequency. Check which one a datasheet quotes before you size the driver swing.

What the driver has to do

RequirementWhy it mattersTypical design response
Large output swingLink gain depends on Vdrive/VπStacked or cascoded output stages to get past the CMOS breakdown limit
Wide, flat bandwidthThe traveling-wave electrode is a lossy transmission lineDistributed or segmented drivers, matched termination
LinearityDriver distortion adds to the modulator's own cosine nonlinearityBack off from compression, consider predistortion
Low noiseDriver noise is amplified by the same link gain as the signalLow-noise front stage ahead of the power stage

Dynamic range: where the cosine catches up with you

Quadrature bias cancels even-order distortion, but the cosine still produces third-order intermodulation. That sets the link's spurious-free dynamic range (SFDR), usually quoted in dB·Hz2/3 so you can compare links measured at different noise bandwidths. A driver that compresses before the modulator does will reduce SFDR on its own. A good co-design keeps the driver's third-order intercept well above the modulator's.

Takeaways

The fiber is rarely the limiting part of an RoF link. The modulator's Vπ sets the gain, its cosine response sets the linearity, and the driver decides how much of both you actually get.

Further reading

  1. C. H. Cox III, Analog Optical Links: Theory and Practice, Cambridge University Press, 2004.

notes.body:
Every receiver datasheet quotes a noise figure, and every RF course derives the Friis formula. What usually gets lost is the intuition: why one stage gets almost all the attention, and why a short piece of cable in the wrong place can cost as much as a bad amplifier. This note works through one example chain to show both.

What noise figure measures

Noise factor F is how much a block degrades the signal-to-noise ratio, measured with a source at the standard temperature T0 = 290 K:

F = SNRin / SNRout,   NF = 10·log10(F) dB(1)

A perfect, noiseless block has F = 1, or 0 dB. A block with NF = 3 dB adds as much noise as the source already had. Note that F is a ratio of powers and NF is the same thing in decibels. The math below uses F, and the datasheets use NF, so you convert back and forth constantly.

Pitfall

Never add noise figures in dB. Convert NF and gain to linear ratios first, apply Friis, then convert the total back to dB.

The Friis formula

For blocks in cascade, each with noise factor Fi and available gain Gi (both as linear ratios):

Ftotal = F1 + (F2 − 1)/G1 + (F3 − 1)/(G1G2) + …(2)

Read it as: each stage's added noise is divided by all the gain in front of it. Once the signal has been amplified, later stages have a much harder time hurting it.

One receiver chain, worked through

Take a simple three-stage receiver: a low-noise amplifier (LNA), a mixer, and an IF amplifier.

StageNFGainF (linear)Term in eq. (2)
LNA1.5 dB20 dB1.4131.413
Mixer10 dB8 dB10.09.0 / 100 = 0.090
IF amplifier4 dB30 dB2.5121.512 / 631 = 0.002
Total1.78 dB1.505

The mixer has a 10 dB noise figure, which looks terrible on its own. Behind 20 dB of LNA gain it adds only about 0.3 dB to the total. The IF amplifier barely registers. The receiver's noise figure is essentially the LNA's noise figure plus a small penalty.

Tip

Think in noise temperature below about 1 dB. Te = 290·(F − 1) K. A 0.5 dB amplifier is about 35 K, which makes small differences between very quiet stages easier to compare.

Where a cable belongs

A passive, lossy block at T0 has a noise factor equal to its loss: a 2 dB loss means NF = 2 dB. Put 2 dB of cable or filter loss before the LNA and it adds directly to the total, giving 3.78 dB. Put the same loss after the LNA and it is divided by 20 dB of gain, adding under 0.02 dB. This is why antennas often have the LNA mounted right at the feed, and why the input filter's loss is fought over so hard.

From noise figure to sensitivity

The thermal noise floor at room temperature is −174 dBm/Hz. A receiver's sensitivity, the weakest signal it can detect, follows directly:

Pmin = −174 dBm/Hz + 10·log10(B) + NF + SNRmin(3)

For our chain with a 20 MHz bandwidth (73 dB) and a demodulator that needs 10 dB SNR: Pmin = −174 + 73 + 1.78 + 10 ≈ −89 dBm. Every dB saved in the LNA, or in the loss in front of it, is a dB of sensitivity.

Pitfall

Check whether a mixer NF is SSB or DSB. A double-sideband figure is about 3 dB lower than the single-sideband figure for the same mixer. Mixing them up hides 3 dB in your budget.

Takeaways

Spend the design effort on the first stage and on anything lossy in front of it. Give the first stage enough gain that later stages stop mattering, but not so much that it compresses on strong signals. Linearity is the other side of this tradeoff, and a good topic for another note.

Further reading

  1. H. T. Friis, “Noise figures of radio receivers,” Proc. IRE, vol. 32, no. 7, pp. 419–422, 1944.
  2. B. Razavi, RF Microelectronics, 2nd ed., Prentice Hall, 2011.

notes.title: Quick dB arithmetic you can do in your head
notes.summary: Five ratios that cover most link-budget sanity checks.
notes.body:
Most link-budget mistakes are caught by a quick mental check. These ratios cover nearly every case:

dBPower ratioVoltage ratio
11.26×1.12×
32×1.41×
64×2×
1010×3.16×
20100×10×

Build anything else from these: 13 dB is 10 + 3, so 20× in power. 7 dB is 10 − 3, so 5×.

Pitfall

Know whether you're in power or voltage. A 6 dB gain doubles the voltage but quadruples the power. In optical links, a 1 dB change in optical power becomes a 2 dB change in RF power after the photodiode, because photocurrent is proportional to optical power and RF power goes as current squared.

notes.title: Sanity-check any receiver with −174 dBm/Hz
notes.summary: The thermal noise floor gives you a sensitivity estimate in ten seconds.
notes.body:
At 290 K, thermal noise is −174 dBm in every hertz of bandwidth. Add 10·log10(B), the noise figure, and the SNR your demodulator needs, and you have the receiver's sensitivity.

Pmin ≈ −174 + 10·log10(B) + NF + SNRmin dBm

Useful bandwidth values to remember: 1 MHz is 60 dB, 20 MHz is 73 dB, 100 MHz is 80 dB, 1 GHz is 90 dB.

Tip

Use it to check a datasheet claim. If a 100 MHz receiver claims −100 dBm sensitivity with 10 dB SNR, the floor alone is −174 + 80 + 10 = −84 dBm before any noise figure. Reaching −100 dBm would need a noise figure of −16 dB, which is impossible. Something in the claim is off.

notes.title: Optics for AI clusters: what stood out at OFC 2026
notes.summary: Faster lanes, linear-drive modules and co-packaged optics, and why each one puts more of the load on analog circuits.
notes.body:
Draft

Written from my OFC 2026 conference summary. Check each claim against the papers before publishing, then delete this box.

At OFC 2026, almost every plenary and keynote framed optical communication around one customer: the AI cluster. Training a large model means moving enormous amounts of data between thousands of accelerators, and the links between them now set both the cluster's speed and a large share of its power bill. For an analog or photonic circuit designer, this is where most of the new work is.

The lane-rate ladder

Optical modules are built from parallel lanes. The industry is moving from 100G per lane to 200G per lane, and 400G-per-lane demonstrations were all over the conference.

Per laneLanesModuleStatus at OFC 2026
100G8800GShipping in volume
200G81.6TThe new baseline
400G83.2TResearch demonstrations and roadmaps

A 200G PAM4 lane runs at roughly 106–113 GBd depending on the error-correction overhead, so each symbol lasts about 9 ps. Every doubling of the lane rate halves that time, and the analog front ends have to keep up.

Where the analog circuits sit

Each lane is a short chain: a driver feeds the modulator, light crosses the fiber, a photodiode converts it back, and a transimpedance amplifier (TIA) and equalizer recover the signal. At these rates the driver's swing and bandwidth, the TIA's noise and bandwidth, and the equalization decide whether the lane closes.

Tip

Bandwidth is not the only spec that matters. Drive swing and energy per bit decide what ships. A modulator with a very wide bandwidth but a high Vπ moves the problem into the driver, which then burns the power you were trying to save.

Modulator options

TechnologyStrengthTrade-off
Thin-film lithium niobateVery wide bandwidth with low drive voltageA separate material platform to integrate
Electro-absorption modulated laser (EML)The workhorse for intensity-modulated datacenter linksLaser and modulator are tied together
Silicon Mach–ZehnderUses CMOS-style fabricationHigher Vπ, so a demanding driver
Silicon microringTiny and very low energy per bitMust be thermally tuned and held on resonance
Barium titanate, silicon-organic hybrid, plasmonicVery low Vπ or very small sizeEarlier in maturity

Three ways to package the optics

ArchitectureWhere the optics sitWhat gets harder for the circuits
Retimed pluggableA module at the front panel with its own DSPThe DSP costs power, but it cleans up the signal in both directions
Linear pluggable optics (LPO)A front-panel module without a DSPThe host SerDes drives the optics directly, so the driver and TIA must be very linear
Co-packaged optics (CPO)Next to the switch or accelerator chipHeat, fiber attach, and usually an external laser source

Pitfall

Co-packaging puts photonics next to the hottest chip in the system. Microring devices drift about 0.07–0.08 nm per kelvin, so in CPO every ring needs a tuning loop like the ones in my microring note.

Beyond links: photonic computing

A smaller set of sessions used light to do the computing itself: photonic tensor cores, photonic Ising machines, and analog all-reduce operations inside a silicon photonic network. These are still research, but they rely on the same building blocks: modulators, rings, photodiodes, and the analog circuits around them.

Takeaways

AI clusters have turned optical interconnect into a power and bandwidth problem at the same time. Faster lanes, linear-drive modules, and co-packaging all push difficulty into the analog front ends and into the control loops that keep photonic devices stable.

Further reading

  1. OFC 2026 technical program, Optica and IEEE, March 2026.

notes.title: Automatic tuning of silicon photonic ring filters
notes.summary: How a small control loop finds each ring's resonance and holds it there despite fabrication variation and temperature drift.
notes.body:
Silicon ring resonators make excellent tunable filters, but they don't stay where you put them. Fabrication variation puts every ring at a slightly different wavelength, and temperature moves it by roughly 0.07–0.08 nm per kelvin, which is about a linewidth for every couple of degrees. A chip with several rings needs an automatic way to find each resonance and hold it there. This note describes, at a high level, how I did that for the reconfigurable filters in my Ph.D. work.

The hardware

Each ring has a thermal phase shifter (a resistive heater) and a small monitor tap that sends part of the ring's light to a photodiode. A 16-channel, 16-bit DAC board that I designed drives the heaters, and a microcontroller reads the photodiodes, runs the search, and steps the tunable laser to the wavelengths of interest.

How the search works

  1. Coarse search. Sweep each ring's heater across a wide range and find the setting where its monitor reads highest, which is where the ring sits on resonance.
  2. Fine search. Sweep a narrow window around that point with smaller steps.
  3. Iterate. Heat from one ring shifts its neighbours, so the whole set is re-tuned in several passes, each with a narrower window, until every ring stops moving.

Each photodiode reading combines many samples through a median filter, so a single noisy sample cannot pull a ring off resonance. When a monitor signal is too weak to trust, the ring keeps its last good setting instead of jumping somewhere new.

Tip

Remember that heater power goes as voltage squared. A linear DAC sweep moves the resonance slowly at low codes and quickly at high codes, so step sizes that work at one end of the range are wrong at the other.

Pitfall

Tune one ring and you detune its neighbours. Thermal crosstalk is why a single pass is never enough. Plan for iterative passes from the start.

What it enabled

The same loop configured band-pass and notch responses on demand and kept them stable during measurements. The results are in my papers on automated tuning of silicon photonic filters and on tunable mm-wave photonic receiver front ends, listed on the Publications page.

More details

This page is an overview. For details on the hardware, the algorithm, or the measured results, email me at engramyrady@gmail.com.
